title: One in Four European Pilots Fly When Tired
paragraphs: Getting through a workday feeling tired can be difficult for anyone. But for airline pilots, it can become a serious safety issue.
A new survey of about 7,200 European pilots found that nearly one in four usually keep flying even when they feel too tired to work.

The survey was done by aviation safety company Baines Simmons for the European Cockpit Association. It found that fatigue is a common problem across European airlines, with little change since 2023, when a similar survey was done.

More than three-quarters of pilots said they'd had at least one "microsleep" while flying in the past four weeks, with one-quarter saying they'd had five or more. A microsleep is a very short, unintentional moment of sleep.

Not getting enough rest is a big part of the problem. Thirty-nine percent of pilots said they "usually" or "always" had too little rest to stop fatigue from building up, while more than half said they had flown in the past three months and later realized they should have reported themselves too tired to fly.
In fact, only 37% said they usually let management know when they feel too tired to fly.
One reason may be fear of how airlines will react. Almost half of pilots said they had flown while fatigued because they were worried about reactions from management.

The survey also found big differences between airlines and countries, with pilots at low-cost airlines reporting more problems. Those working for airlines in Ireland and Malta were among the most likely to fear negative reactions from management, while Finland and the Netherlands had some of the strongest fatigue-reporting cultures.
The European Cockpit Association said airlines and aviation authorities need to do more to reduce fatigue risks, instead of leaving pilots to manage them on their own.
